Qatar Floods Disrupt Energy Operations and Supply Chains as Government Mobilizes Response

Severe flooding across Qatar has brought widespread disruption to the country’s economic activity, with energy operations, supply chains, and transport infrastructure all affected. Torrential rains began late Sunday and continued into Tuesday, overwhelming drainage systems in Doha and surrounding cities. The event is the most significant flooding Qatar has experienced in over a decade, according to local meteorological authorities.

QatarEnergy, the state-owned energy company, said in a statement that it had “temporarily halted certain non-essential operations” at Ras Laffan Industrial City due to inundated roads and logistical bottlenecks. “Our first priority is the safety of our personnel,” the company said, adding that core operations continue but with “reduced staffing and restricted movement.” The company did not provide estimates of production impact but said it was working closely with emergency services to restore access.

The floods have also disrupted major highways and caused power outages in several districts of Doha, delaying deliveries of critical goods and construction materials. The Qatar Chamber of Commerce reported that “hundreds of shipments” have been delayed at Hamad Port, with containers of perishable goods among those at risk. The port remains operational but is experiencing slowdowns due to waterlogged access roads and staff shortages.

Ahmed Al-Kuwari, an economist at Doha Financial Strategies, said the flooding exposed vulnerabilities in Qatar’s urban infrastructure. “Qatar’s rapid urban expansion has sometimes outpaced upgrades to stormwater drainage. The economic impact could be significant if disruptions persist beyond a few days, especially in logistics and energy,” he said.

The Ministry of Commerce and Industry announced that it is coordinating with retailers and suppliers to prevent shortages of essential goods. “We are monitoring inventories and have activated emergency procedures to ensure the continued flow of food and medicines,” a spokesperson said. Some supermarkets in Doha reported runs on bottled water and basic staples, but government officials urged residents not to panic.

Industrial activity outside the energy sector has also been hampered. Qatar Steelworks, a major manufacturer, said it had suspended operations due to flooding at its plant and difficulties transporting workers and materials. The Qatar Business Council called for urgent government support to assist affected small and medium-sized enterprises.

Flights in and out of Hamad International Airport are facing delays, with Qatar’s Civil Aviation Authority advising travelers to check with their airlines for updates.

Meteorologists forecast further rain through Wednesday, raising concerns about additional flooding. Emergency crews are working to clear critical roads and deploy pumps in the worst-hit neighborhoods. “The situation remains dynamic,” said Saad Al-Mohannadi, head of Qatar’s National Emergency Operations Center. “We urge residents to stay indoors and follow official guidance as we respond to this unprecedented weather event.”
